title: Why other data models exist: Bigtable, Dynamo and the families
goal: By the end you can name the three things the relational model makes hard (changing the shape of records, keeping related data together, growing past one machine), tell schema-on-read from schema-on-write, read a sorted row key and a hash-ring preference list, and place any store by its data model rather than its brand.

warmup.q: A document store accepts merchant records with no declared schema. Two years in, the team splits `name` into `legalName` and `tradingName` for new merchants. Where does the schema of the old records live now?
options: Nowhere: a schemaless store has no schema
In the code that reads the records, which has to handle both shapes
In the store, which rewrote the old records when the first new-shape record arrived
In an index the store built from the field names it has seen
warmup.why: The store kept each record exactly as it was written, so old merchants still have `name` and new ones have the two new fields. Something still has to know that, and with no declared schema it's every piece of code that reads merchants. That's schema-on-read. No store rewrites old records on its own, and indexes are built on the fields you name, not on a guess about shapes.

sections.h: Tables make three things hard: changing shape, keeping data together, growing past one machine
sections.body:
The SQL track built everything on one model. A table holds rows that all have the same named, typed columns, the rows have no order, and a query says what it wants while the optimizer decides how to get it. Edgar Codd proposed the model in 1970 so that programs would stop breaking every time someone changed how data was laid out on disk, and by the mid-1980s it was the default. The SQL track ended with Kotlin code reaching that model through JDBC, a connection pool and numbered Flyway migrations.

So why store data any other way? Because the model makes three things hard, and a payments system hits all three.

The first is changing shape. Every row has the same columns, so every new field is a migration. In PostgreSQL `ALTER TABLE merchant ADD COLUMN vat_id text` is quick, because it only changes the catalog. Splitting `name` into `legal_name` and `trading_name` is an `UPDATE` that rewrites every row, and changing a column's type usually copies the whole table. Merchant onboarding forms that differ by country and change every quarter become a migration every quarter, or a wide table of mostly NULLs.

The second is keeping things together. The payment screen shows a payment, its fraud checks, its captures and its refunds. Normalized, that's four tables, so one payment's rows sit in four places on disk, and the screen costs four index lookups or a four-way join. Stored as one record, the screen is one read of one place. That property is called locality: data that is read together is stored together.

The third is growing past one machine. One primary takes every insert. Say your Oracle primary handles 8,000 payment inserts a second at 70% CPU, and the Black Friday forecast says 25,000. A bigger machine (scaling up) is the right first answer for most systems, but there is a biggest machine, and while it fails over to a standby every authorization waits. The other answer is to split the data over many machines, each holding one part, called a partition (some products say shard). That's scaling out. Now every read and write must first find the machine that holds its key, each key needs copies on other machines (replicas) so one dead machine doesn't take it offline, and a join or a transfer across two machines needs a network round trip: about 0.5 ms inside a data centre, about 70 ms between regions.

**Every family in this track gives up something tables have, usually joins, multi-row transactions or a declared schema, to make one of these three cheap.** That's the picture for the whole track. The two papers that started it came from Google and Amazon. Bigtable (OSDI 2006) keeps all keys sorted and cuts them into ranges, one server per range. Dynamo (SOSP 2007) hashes each key onto a ring and keeps live copies on several machines, so a write never waits for a dead one. The figure shows both, and sections 3 and 4 build them.

sections.h: Schemaless means the schema moved into the code
sections.body:
Stores without a declared schema are often called schemaless. The name is wrong. Some code still has to know that a merchant has a name and a country. If the database doesn't check that, the code that reads the data assumes it.

So a schema can live in one of two places. Schema-on-write means the database checks every record against a declared structure when it's written, and rejects what doesn't fit. A table is schema-on-write: an `INSERT` of a text value into a `bigint` column fails. Schema-on-read means the database stores whatever arrives, and each reader decides what the bytes mean. A JSON document store with no validator is schema-on-read. It's static versus dynamic typing, applied to data, and neither wins everywhere.

Take the name split again. In a document store you write new merchants in the new shape, `legalName` and `tradingName`, and leave the old ones alone. The read code handles both: use `tradingName` if it's there, else `legalName`, else the old `name`. No migration ran and nothing was locked. The price arrives later. Every reader, in every service, must know every shape the data has ever had. And a typo in an import job, `Name` with a capital N, is stored without complaint and turns up as a blank on a screen months later.

Schema-on-read wins when records really differ: forms that vary by country, payloads from card networks or partners that change without asking you. Schema-on-write wins when every record has the same structure, because then the database documents it and enforces it in one place. The line is blurring from both sides. MongoDB 9.0 added a validation level, `constraint`, that guarantees every document in a collection passes its rules, and PostgreSQL keeps schema-on-read documents in `jsonb` columns, as the SQL track's lesson on JSONB showed. Lesson 6 puts the two side by side.

Before you run it, predict the name it prints for each merchant.
Run it from the `labs` folder. Then add a fifth record in a shape the reader doesn't know, such as `{"_id": "M-0080", "shopName": "Kiosk 9"}`, and run it again.

try.expect:
```text
M-0042  Northwind Bikes              fields=[name, country]
M-0051  Volt                         fields=[legalName, tradingName, country]
M-0063  Kools GmbH                   fields=[legalName, country, vatId]
```

The store took all four records without a word. M-0051 shows its trading name and M-0063 falls back to its legal name, because the reader knows those shapes. With schema-on-write, that insert would have failed at once, inside the job that made the mistake. Your fifth record prints `<no name>` too, until you teach `displayName` about it.

sections.h: Bigtable: keep the keys sorted, then cut them into ranges
sections.body:
Take one question, "show merchant M-0042's payments from today", over a table of 2 billion payments. Build a store that answers it cheaply, one version at a time.

Version 1 is a hash map from key to value, like Java's `HashMap`. It finds one key fast. But a hash map keeps its keys in no useful order, so "every key that starts with M-0042" means visiting all 2 billion entries.

Version 2 keeps the keys sorted, like Java's `TreeMap`. Sorted here means lexicographic order: compare two keys character by character, the way a dictionary orders words. Now design the key so the question becomes a prefix. In `M-0042#2026-11-07T08:15:03#pay-81701`, the merchant comes first, then the time, then the payment id. All of M-0042's payments sit next to each other in time order, and one day is one unbroken run. To read it, the store jumps to the first key at or after `M-0042#2026-11-07` and walks forward until a key stops matching. That walk is a range read. Its cost depends on how many rows it returns, not on the size of the table. Put the payment id first and the same question visits every row again. **The row key decides which questions are cheap.**

Version 3 spreads the sorted list over machines. Cut it into contiguous pieces of about 100 to 200 MB; Bigtable calls a piece a tablet, and each tablet server serves many tablets. Because the pieces follow key order, a range read touches one tablet, or two when it crosses a boundary. A tablet that grows too big is split in two. When a server dies, the master (one coordinating server) gives its tablets to other servers, which load the files from GFS, Google's distributed file system.

Version 4 gives the value some structure. With one opaque blob per key, changing a payment's status means rewriting the whole payment, and the old status is gone. So Bigtable addresses a value by three things. The paper writes it in one line:

```text
(row:string, column:string, time:int64) -> string
```

A column name has two parts, `family:qualifier`, such as `pay:status` or `risk:score`. You declare families up front. Qualifiers are free, and a row stores only the columns it actually wrote: a missing column costs nothing, not even a NULL. That's what the paper means by sparse. So a new kind of column needs no migration: the next write just uses a new qualifier. Each cell keeps several versions under 64-bit timestamps, newest first, and a per-family setting keeps only the last n versions or only recent ones.

One rule limits what you can build on top: every read or write under a single row key is atomic (it happens completely or not at all, and no reader sees half of it), however many columns it touches. Nothing is atomic across rows.

How does a server insert into a sorted structure fast? It appends each write to a commit log, a file on disk that only grows, so the write survives a crash. Then it adds the write to a sorted buffer in memory, the memtable. A full memtable is written out as an immutable sorted file, an SSTable, and background compactions merge SSTables. That design is the LSM tree (log-structured merge tree). HBase, Google Cloud Bigtable and Cassandra all store data this way; lesson 5 watches Cassandra do it, and the Storage engines track builds one.

sections.h: Dynamo: hash keys onto a ring and keep writing through failures
sections.body:
Amazon's requirement was blunt: "Add to Cart" must succeed even while servers and network links fail. It measured latency at the 99.9th percentile (the time that 999 of every 1,000 requests beat), so a store that stalled whenever one server died wasn't good enough. Dynamo calls each server a node. Build it up one version at a time.

Version 1 puts one copy of each key on node number `hash(key) mod S`, where S is the number of nodes. A hash function such as MD5 turns any key into a big number that looks random, so keys spread evenly. This breaks the day you add a node. Going from 4 nodes to 5 changes the remainder for most keys: of every 20 consecutive hash values, only 4 give the same remainder mod 4 and mod 5, so 80% of all keys move at once.

Version 2 uses a ring. Lay every possible MD5 value around a circle. Hash each node's name to place the node on the circle, and hash each key the same way. A key belongs to the first node you meet walking clockwise from the key. Adding a node now only takes keys from one neighbour: with 5 nodes of equal share, about a fifth of the keys move instead of 80%. That trick is consistent hashing.

Version 3 adds copies, because with one copy a dead node makes its keys unreachable. The first node clockwise, the coordinator, stores the key and sends it on to the next nodes clockwise, N nodes in all. The paper calls them the key's preference list, and N is typically 3.

Version 4 stops waiting for everyone. A write that waited for all 3 copies would be as slow as the slowest node. So Dynamo waits for W of them, and a read asks R of them; with R + W > N, say 2 and 2 of 3, every read overlaps the latest write on at least one node. These are quorums, and the Replication track's lesson on leaderless replication runs them on a Cassandra cluster.

Version 5 keeps writing when a home node is down. The write goes to the first N healthy nodes clockwise instead. The stand-in keeps the write with a hint naming the real owner and hands it over when the owner returns. The paper calls this a sloppy quorum with hinted handoff. The stepper walks through versions 2 to 5.

The price: during a failure, two writes to the same cart can land on different nodes, and the copies disagree. Dynamo doesn't pick a winner. It tags each version with a vector clock, a short list of (node, counter) pairs, and a read that finds two versions where neither has seen the other returns both for the cart service to merge. An added item is never lost; as the paper admits, a deleted item can come back. The Replication track's lesson on concurrent writes builds vector clocks.

DynamoDB is not Dynamo. Its 2022 USENIX paper says the two share most of a name and little of the architecture. A DynamoDB partition keeps its copies in several availability zones (separate data centres in one region), and the copies elect a leader with Multi-Paxos, a consensus protocol that lets copies agree on one leader and one order of writes (the Consistency and consensus track builds Raft, a close relative). Only the leader takes writes and strongly consistent reads, so there are no vector clocks for your code to merge. Lessons 3 and 4 use DynamoDB.

sections.h: The families: what you store decides what you can ask
sections.body:
Placement decides where data lives. The data model decides which questions are cheap, and what the store can check for you. Build the families up from the simplest one.

Key-value is the simplest model: `put(key, value)` and `get(key)`, with the value opaque to the store. Dynamo is this model, and so is Redis (the Caching track). Stonebraker and Pavlo, in their 2024 survey of the data models of the last twenty years, name the catch: once a value has several fields, your code parses it, there are no secondary indexes, and every join happens in the application. That's why DynamoDB grew into a store of items with named attributes and a sort key (lessons 3 and 4).

Add a sorted second part to the key, let each row carry its own columns, and you get Bigtable's wide-column model. The name misleads. A wide-column store isn't a column store: a column store keeps each column's values together on disk, so a report can read one column of a billion rows (the Storage engines track builds one), while a wide-column store keeps each partition's rows together. The survey calls it the document model cut down to one level of nesting. Cassandra is this track's example (lesson 5).

Let the store see inside the value, a JSON-like document with nested fields and arrays, and you get the document model: one record per object tree, so locality comes free (lesson 6). Store the relationships themselves and you get the graph model, nodes such as accounts and devices joined by edges such as "uses device" (lessons 7 to 9). Search, time-series and vector stores are mostly one special index over these models: the survey calls a vector database a document database with a nearest-neighbour index.

| Family | You store | You find it by | In this track |
|---|---|---|---|
| Key-value | a value, or an item of named attributes | its key, or a sorted run inside one partition | DynamoDB, lessons 3 and 4 |
| Wide-column | rows in partitions, sorted inside, columns per row | the partition key, then a slice of the sort order | Cassandra 5.0, lesson 5 |
| Document | JSON-like trees with nested fields | any field you index | MongoDB 9.0 and PostgreSQL `jsonb`, lesson 6 |
| Graph | nodes and the relationships between them | a start node, then a walk along edges | SQL, Neo4j, triples and Datalog, lessons 7 to 9 |
| Search, time-series, vector | text, measurements, embeddings | an inverted index, a time bucket, nearest neighbours | the Storage engines track |

The walls are coming down from both sides. By the end of the 2010s nearly every NoSQL store had a SQL-like language (Cassandra's CQL, DynamoDB's PartiQL), while PostgreSQL learned to store documents and Oracle to run graph queries. So read each family as a model, a promise about which questions are cheap, rather than as a product.

Two myths are worth dropping now. "NoSQL means no schema": every store here makes you declare a key, Cassandra tables have typed columns, and MongoDB 9.0 can hold every document to its rules. "NoSQL means no transactions": DynamoDB transactions cover up to 100 items, MongoDB has multi-document transactions, and Cassandra 5.0 has lightweight transactions on one partition. The Transactions track's lesson on transactions in NoSQL covers what they cost.

Relational still wins when the questions aren't known in advance, when reports need joins, and when an invariant spans many rows, like a ledger that must balance.

try.title: Sort five payment needs into families
steps: For each need, write down the family you would reach for first and the key you would look things up by. Commit to an answer before you open the expected result.

(a) Check an idempotency key in under 5 ms, 20,000 times a second. (b) Store merchant onboarding forms whose fields differ by country and change every quarter. (c) Find accounts that share a device or a phone number with a flagged fraudster, up to three hops away. (d) Keep every card authorization for 13 months and show one card's last 50, newest first. (e) Find the merchant whose name someone typed as "Nrthwind Bikes".
try.expect: (a) Key-value: DynamoDB (or Redis) keyed by the idempotency key, one lookup per check. (b) Document: MongoDB, one document per application, with a validation rule for the fields every country shares. (c) Graph: Neo4j, start at the flagged account and walk "uses device" and "uses phone" relationships. (d) Wide-column, or key-value with a sort key: partition by card, sort by time descending, read 50 from the top. (e) Search: an inverted index with fuzzy matching, such as OpenSearch. If you put (d) in Oracle, you're not wrong at small volume. The question is where one primary stops keeping up with the writes.

refs.title: Stonebraker and Pavlo, What Goes Around Comes Around... And Around (SIGMOD Record, June 2024, PDF)

analogy: Bigtable is a giant phone book. Every entry is sorted by name and the book is split into volumes, A to C, D to F, each on its own shelf. Everyone named Kools is one flip and a short read down a page. Everyone living on Main Street means reading every volume, because the book isn't sorted by street. Dynamo is a round table of clerks. Each clerk takes the folders whose numbers fall between them and the clerk on their left, and passes copies to the next two clerks round the table. When a clerk is out sick, the next one takes the folder with a sticky note saying whose it really is. The analogy breaks in two places: a phone book is printed once, while Bigtable merges new entries into its sorted files all the time, and Dynamo's clerks can briefly hold two different versions of the same folder without noticing.
in_your_world: Your authorization path in Quarkus writes to Oracle, where one primary takes every insert. Look at the idempotency check that runs before each authorization: one lookup by one key, maybe 20,000 times a second at peak, and the key is useless after a day. That is a key-value access pattern, and it's often the first table a payments team moves to DynamoDB or Redis. The merchant onboarding forms, different per country and changed every quarter, are the classic case for documents. The ledger, with its rule that every transfer's debits and credits balance and its month-end reports, stays relational. A Kafka consumer that builds each merchant's daily payment view fits a wide-column table keyed by merchant and day. Choose per access pattern, not per company. The rest of this track builds that habit.
mistake: The most common mistake is choosing a NoSQL store for its name and then modeling it like the relational schema you already have: one table per entity, foreign keys as plain attributes, and the queries worked out later. The store has no joins and no optimizer to rescue you, so every new question becomes a full scan or a second copy of the data. People do it because the relational habit runs deep and the tables look familiar. The fix is the next lesson: write the access patterns down first, then design keys so each one is a single lookup or a single range read.

compare.note: The relational row has a fixed set of typed columns, keeps one current value per column, and lets you index and query any column. The Bigtable row has whatever columns it wrote, keeps several timestamped versions per cell, and can only be found by its row key or a range of row keys. That is why the row key carries the merchant and the time: in Bigtable the key is the query.

worked.title: Design a row key for "a merchant's latest payments"

steps.say: Write the question down first: show merchant M-0042's 50 most recent payments. A Bigtable-style store does two cheap things, get one row and read a range of rows in key order. So the answer has to be one range.
steps.code: access pattern: merchant = M-0042, newest first, stop after 50

steps.say: First try: the payment id as the row key. Each payment has a unique key, but one merchant's payments are scattered across the whole key space, so the question becomes a full table scan.
steps.code:
pay-81655  pay-81690  pay-81701  pay-81712  pay-81720 ...
# M-0042's rows are mixed in with every other merchant's

steps.say: Second try: merchant, then time, then payment id. Now one prefix read covers exactly M-0042's payments. But they come out oldest first, so the newest 50 sit at the end of the range, and a forward read passes every older payment to reach them.
steps.code:
fun rowKey(merchantId: String, at: Instant, paymentId: String) =
    "$merchantId#$at#$paymentId"   // oldest first within the merchant

steps.say: Third try: store the time reversed. `Long.MAX_VALUE` minus the epoch millis gets smaller as time moves on, so the newest payment sorts first. Pad it to 19 digits so it compares correctly as text. A prefix read of `M-0042#` with a limit of 50 now stops after exactly 50 rows.

Check the price. All of one merchant's new payments now land at the start of the same key range, which lives on one tablet. For a merchant taking thousands of payments a second, that one tablet server takes every write. The Partitioning track's lesson on hot keys spreads a hot key across several ranges and merges them on read.

lab.title: Build a tiny Bigtable: one sorted map of cells
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. All seven fail with `NotImplementedError`. No Docker needed: this lab is plain Kotlin.
Write `CellKey.compareTo`: row ascending, then column ascending, then timestamp descending. The first test passes.
Write `put`. Reject a column whose family isn't declared (`familyOf` is given), insert the cell, then delete every version of that cell beyond `maxVersions`.
Write `versions`. Start at `CellKey(row, column, Long.MAX_VALUE)` and walk forward while the row and column still match. `get` is built on it, so its test passes too.
Write `readRow` and `scan` the same way: jump to the first possible key, walk forward, stop at the first key that no longer matches. Run the tests until all seven pass.
hints: Why `Long.MAX_VALUE`? Timestamps sort in reverse, so the biggest timestamp is the smallest key of a cell. `CellKey(row, "", Long.MAX_VALUE)` is the first possible key of a whole row, because `""` sorts before every column name.
`cells.tailMap(from, true)` is a live view from `from` to the end of the map. Walk it with `.entries.asSequence().takeWhile { ... }` and you never touch the rest of the table.
In `readRow`, compare the row with `==`. Row `pay-10` starts with `pay-1`, and the test checks that you don't pick it up. In `scan`, `startsWith` is right, because there you want the prefix.
To drop old versions in `put`, collect the extra keys into a list first, then remove them. Removing entries while you iterate over a view of the same map throws `ConcurrentModificationException`.

recap: The relational model makes three things hard: changing the shape of records, keeping related data together (locality), and growing past one machine. Each family gives up joins, multi-row transactions or a declared schema to make one of them cheap.

Schemaless means schema-on-read: the store keeps whatever arrives and every reader carries the schema. Schema-on-write checks each record once, in the database. Use the first when records really differ.
Bigtable (2006) is one sparse map sorted by row key, cut into tablets: the row key decides where data lives and which questions are a cheap range read, and only single-row operations are atomic.

Dynamo (2007) hashes keys onto a ring of equal nodes, copies each key to N nodes and keeps writing through failures with sloppy quorums. DynamoDB shares the name and hash partitioning, but each partition has a Multi-Paxos leader.

Key-value, wide-column, document and graph are models, not products. Wide-column is not columnar, a vector store is a document store plus an index, and "no schema" and "no transactions" are both out of date.

quiz.q: A Bigtable-style table uses the row key `paymentId#merchantId`. Support asks for merchant M-0042's payments from today. What does the store have to do?
options: Look the merchant up in the secondary index Bigtable keeps for every part of the key
Read every row, because the merchant isn't a prefix of the row key
Read one tablet, because all of a merchant's rows live on the same tablet
Filter by the column family on the server without reading any rows
quiz.why: Rows are sorted by the whole row key as a string, so only a prefix of the key gives a contiguous range. With the payment id first, M-0042's rows are scattered across every tablet. Bigtable keeps no secondary indexes, and column families group columns, not rows.

quiz.q: Dynamo with N = 3. Walking clockwise from a key's hash you meet nodes D, E, F, G. D is down when a write for the key arrives. Where does the write go?
options: Nowhere: the write is rejected until D comes back
To E and F only, with W lowered to 2 for this write
To C, the node just before the key on the ring
To E, F and G, and G keeps a hint that the data belongs to D
quiz.why: Dynamo writes to the first N healthy nodes on the ring. G isn't a home replica for this key, so it stores the write with a hint and hands it to D when D recovers. Rejecting the write would break "always writeable", and the ring is only ever walked clockwise.

quiz.q: Which statement about Amazon DynamoDB is true?
options: It's the 2007 Dynamo paper's system offered as a managed service
It returns conflicting versions to your code, tagged with vector clocks
Each partition's replicas elect a leader, and the leader takes the writes
It doesn't use a partition key; any node can store any item
quiz.why: The 2022 DynamoDB paper describes a Multi-Paxos replication group per partition, where only the leader serves writes and strongly consistent reads. DynamoDB kept Dynamo's name and hash partitioning but not its leaderless design or vector clocks.

quiz.q: A colleague calls Cassandra "a column store, so it's great for scanning one column across all payments for a report". What's wrong with that?
options: Cassandra is wide-column: it keeps each partition's rows together, so a report over one column still reads whole partitions on every node
Nothing: wide-column and columnar mean the same thing
Cassandra stores each column in a separate table, so the report needs a join
Cassandra has no columns, only opaque values
quiz.why: A column store (the kind the Storage engines track builds) keeps each column's values together on disk, which is what makes one-column scans cheap. A wide-column store groups rows by partition key and sorts them inside the partition; Stonebraker and Pavlo call it a document model with one level of nesting. Cassandra columns are typed and named, and there are no joins at all.

quiz.q: A fraud team wants accounts that share a device or a phone with a flagged account, up to three hops away, in under 100 ms. Which family fits first?
options: Key-value, keyed by account id
Wide-column, partitioned by device id
Graph, starting at the flagged account and walking shared identifiers
Document, with each account's devices embedded
quiz.why: The question is a walk along relationships of unknown length, which is exactly what a graph store does from a start node. In the other families each hop is a separate lookup or an extra copy of the data, and three hops multiply them.

flashcards.front: What is Bigtable's data model, in one line?
flashcards.back: A sparse, sorted map: `(row:string, column:string, time:int64) -> string`.
On write: the database checks every record against a declared structure and rejects what doesn't fit. On read: it stores whatever arrives, and the reading code assumes a structure.
A contiguous range of rows: the unit Bigtable serves, splits and moves between servers. About 100 to 200 MB by default in the paper.

flashcards.front: In Dynamo, what is a key's preference list?
flashcards.back: The nodes that store the key: the first node clockwise from the key's hash (the coordinator) and the next ones clockwise, N nodes in all.

flashcards.front: What does Dynamo do when a home replica is down during a write?
flashcards.back: Sloppy quorum: it writes to the first N healthy nodes. The stand-in keeps a hint and hands the data back when the owner returns (hinted handoff).

flashcards.front: Is DynamoDB the system from the 2007 Dynamo paper?
flashcards.back: No. It shares the name and hash partitioning, but each partition has a Multi-Paxos leader that takes writes and strongly consistent reads.

flashcards.front: Is a wide-column store a column store?
flashcards.back: No. A column store keeps each column's values together for analytics. A wide-column store keeps each partition's rows together, sorted, with columns per row.

terms.plain: Spread the data over more machines instead of buying one bigger machine (scaling up).
One part of a split-up dataset, held by one machine or one small group of machines. Some products say shard.
A copy of a partition's data on another machine, so the data survives and stays reachable when one machine dies.
Bigtable sorts rows by row key and cuts the sorted rows into tablets, contiguous ranges of about 100 to 200 MB, one server each.
A group of columns declared up front, written `family:qualifier`. Qualifiers can differ per row.
Keys and nodes hashed onto one circle; a key belongs to the first node clockwise. Adding a node moves only its neighbour's keys.
Whether the reading code or the database holds a record to its expected structure.
Storing data that is read together in one place, so one read fetches it all.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate says: "Let's move merchant onboarding to a document store. It's schemaless, so we never have to think about schemas again." Explain what's right, what's wrong, and what you'd do.
explain_back.answer: The right part: onboarding forms differ by country and change every quarter, and a document store can take each merchant in the shape it arrives, with no migration and no table full of NULLs. The wrong part: the schema doesn't go away, it moves. Schemaless really means schema-on-read, so every service that reads merchants must know every shape the data has ever had, and a typo from an import job is stored without complaint and shows up months later as a blank field. I'd use the document store for the forms, put a validator on the fields every country shares (MongoDB 9.0's `constraint` level even guarantees every stored document passes), and keep one reader module that maps all known shapes to one Kotlin class, so the knowledge lives in one place.

deeper.body:
Dynamo's paper has a table that maps each problem to the technique that solves it. It's the best one-page map of the distributed ideas you'll meet later in the course:

| Problem | Technique | Where you meet it again |
|---|---|---|
| Partitioning | Consistent hashing | The Partitioning track: consistent hashing and hot keys |
| Highly available writes | Vector clocks, merged on read | The Replication track: concurrent writes |
| Temporary failures | Sloppy quorum and hinted handoff | The Replication track: leaderless replication |
| Permanent failures | Anti-entropy with Merkle trees | The Replication track: leaderless replication |
| Membership and failure detection | Gossip | The Partitioning track: inside a Cassandra cluster |

Bigtable leans on other Google systems that the paper describes briefly. It stores its log and SSTable files in GFS, a distributed file system, so a tablet server holds no data that would be lost with its disk. It uses Chubby, a lock service whose five replicas agree using Paxos, to make sure only one master runs and to track which tablet servers are alive. When a tablet server dies, the master gives its tablets to other servers, which replay the commit log from GFS. That is a sharp contrast with Dynamo: Bigtable recovers by moving responsibility to another server, while Dynamo keeps several live copies and keeps writing.

Abadi's PACELC paper, which the Consistency and consensus track's first lesson reads properly, classifies these systems by two trade-offs: what they give up during a network partition, and what they trade between latency and consistency the rest of the time. By that paper's 2012 labels, Dynamo and Cassandra choose availability and low latency, while Bigtable and HBase choose consistency in both cases.

For the history behind section 1, read chapter 3 of *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, 2nd edition (Kleppmann and Riccomini). It walks from Codd's relations through documents and graphs and treats schema-on-read as a trade-off, not a feature. Stonebraker and Pavlo's 2024 survey is the sharper read: section by section it argues that each non-relational model either stayed a niche or grew back into SQL.
